[MUQATIL:104:1-5/r2] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | The narrative says the man swore he could distribute his wealth throughout Quraysh while alive without exhausting it, and challenged the threat of poverty.
[MUQATIL:104:1-5/r3] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | He is told that the One who gave him his wealth can take it away; this affects him, and he begins counting his possessions.
[MUQATIL:104:1-5/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | reports | He tells Muhammad that even if all his counted wealth were bread it would not run out, and the condemnation in Sūrat al-Humazah is revealed in response.
[MUQATIL:104:1-5/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | He repeats that the man's wealth will not make him immortal.
[MUQATIL:104:1-9/r5] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | He imagines his wealth will preserve him from death until the wealth itself is spent.
[MUQATIL:104:1-9/r6] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | God rejects this belief: neither his wealth nor his children will make him immortal.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابعلمكلفعلتعداكإلىغيرك)#675/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sibawayh groups three conjugation patterns as shared by transitive and intransitive verbs, including faʿala-yafʿilu, faʿila-yafʿalu, and faʿala-yafʿulu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابعلمكلفعلتعداكإلىغيرك)#675/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Intransitive verbs have a fourth pattern, faʿula-yafʿulu, which transitive verbs do not share; Sibawayh says there is no transitive faʿultuhu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابعلمكلفعلتعداكإلىغيرك)#675/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The fourth pattern marks intransitivity; the other three past-tense patterns and their corresponding imperfect patterns are shared across transitive and intransitive verbs.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابعلمكلفعلتعداكإلىغيرك)#675/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sibawayh lists ḥasiba-yaḥsabu among verbs with a nonstandard imperfect vowel; the fatḥa form is sound and more analogical.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابعلمكلفعلتعداكإلىغيرك)#675/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sibawayh cites al-Farazdaq’s line to attest the imperfect yanʿamu with ḍamma, describing guests’ delight or comfort.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابعلمكلفعلتعداكإلىغيرك)#675/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A few verbs occur with ḍamma in the imperfect despite their usual pattern; Sibawayh gives faḍila-yafḍulu and māta-tamūtu and notes more analogical forms.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابعلمكلفعلتعداكإلىغيرك)#675/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · الخليل | reports | Al-Khalīl calls the reported kāda-takādu pattern irregular, comparing it with the irregular faḍila-yafḍulu class.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماهذهالحروففيهفاءات)#709/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | For verbs with initial hamza, such as amara-yaʾmuru and akala-yaʾkulu, Sibawayh explains the imperfect vowel by analogy with assimilation and the treatment of a medial hamza.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماهذهالحروففيهفاءات)#709/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | He also relates the following vowel to how a medial hamza and its counterparts would open a neighboring letter, while avoiding an opening that conflicts with a quiescent initial hamza.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماهذهالحروففيهفاءات)#709/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sibawayh explains abā-yaʾbā by analogy with qaraʾa-yaqraʾu, while also allowing an analogy with ḥasiba-yaḥsabu.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماهذهالحروففيهفاءات)#709/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Jabā-yajbā and qalā-yaqlā follow the qaraʾa pattern, but Sibawayh says these forms are known only from weakly transmitted usage.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماهذهالحروففيهفاءات)#709/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The forms ʿamara-yaʿmuru and yaḥzuru follow the regular analogy; Sibawayh gives them as better-attested cases.
[SIBAWAYH:(هذابابماهذهالحروففيهفاءات)#709/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Sibawayh cites waʿadahu-yaʿiduhu as an analogy for opening after a quiescent initial radical, but says ʿaḍaḍtu-taʿaḍḍu is not well attested.
[FARRA:v3p289#2/r5] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | أخلده means “will make him live forever”; the past form can express a future result, as when one says a sinner entered Hell meaning Hell is due for him.
[AKHFASH:v2p584/r2] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | يحسب أن ماله أخلده كلا لينبذن means that he and his wealth will be cast into the Crusher.

[WAHIDI-QT:104:3/r1] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · author | holds | He thinks his wealth has made him immortal in this world, so that he will not die.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p218/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | In comparison, the speaker focuses on the quality shared by two things and disregards their other differences.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p218/r2] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Calling Zayd like a lion gives him a measured share of bravery; calling him the lion makes a maximal claim, either nearly true or hyperbolic.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p218/r3] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The lion's name is grounded chiefly in courage; its other features and qualities are secondary to that defining attribute.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p218/r4] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | One use of “he is” identifies one person known by either of two names.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p218/r5] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | A second use of “he is” asserts complete likeness and denies any difference or disparity between two things.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p218/r6] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The complete-likeness sense derives from identity: two fully similar things can make a viewer at different times think he has seen the same thing.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p218/r7] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | Applied to the lion comparison, focusing only on courage and denying any difference between the two forms the hyperbolic sense of calling the person “himself.”

rts | Al-Ḥasan visited a wealthy man who said he had saved thousands against hard times, harsh rulers, calamities, and fear of poverty; al-Ḥasan replied that he was leaving it to people who would neither thank nor excuse him.
[KASHSHAF:104:3/r6] KASHSHAF, d. 538 · author | rejects | Kallā rebukes the miser’s assumption that wealth makes him immortal.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p801/r16] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Akhledahu and khalladahu both mean that wealth lengthened his hopes until he imagined it would keep him alive forever.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p801/r17] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Alternatively, he builds fortified homes, plants trees, and develops the land as though wealth made him live forever.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p801/r18] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | A further interpretation makes the wording an ironic allusion to good works, which truly make their doer abide in bliss; wealth does not.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p801/r19] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | reports | Reports say al-Akhnas had either four thousand or ten thousand dinars.
[KASHSHAF-FULL:v4p801/r21] KASHSHAF-FULL, d. 538 · author | holds | Kalla rebukes the man's belief that wealth made him immortal.
[IBNATIYYA:104:3/r1] IBNATIYYA, d. 542 · author | holds | He imagines wealth is the substance and support of life: it preserved him through his lifetime and will keep preserving him.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p521#3/r2] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · author | holds | The miser thinks wealth is the substance and support of his life: it preserved him so far and, he imagines, will preserve him forever.
[IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p521#3/r4] IBNATIYYA-FULL, d. 542 · الأعرج وأبو جعفر وشيبة | reports | They read يَحْسَب with fatḥa on س.
[TABRISI:104:1-9#2/r15] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | holds | The hoarder thinks wealth will keep him alive and protect him from death; the past verb means the future because “he thinks” governs it, and he acts as though hoping for immortality despite knowing everyone dies.
[TABRISI:104:1-9#2/r16] TABRISI, d. 548 · author | reports | Alternatively, “made immortal” means that wealth caused immortality, as when someone is said to have perished once the cause arose even before death occurred.
[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v9p229/r1] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · author | holds | “Made him immortal” means “will make him immortal”: the person thinks wealth will protect him from death and acts as if he will not die.
[RAZI:104:3/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Al-Rāzī says akhladahu and khalladahu have the same meaning, then records four interpretations of the claim that wealth makes its possessor endure.
[RAZI:104:3/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | Al-Ḥasan’s interpretation is that wealth lengthens the person’s hopes until, through heedlessness, he thinks it has made him immortal; the past tense pictures immortality as an already-secured guarantee against death.
[RAZI:104:3/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | A second interpretation is that he constructs durable buildings of brick and plaster as someone expecting to live on or to be remembered after death.
[RAZI:104:3/r4] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | A third view says he loves wealth so intensely that he imagines losing any of it would kill him and preserves it to stay alive; al-Rāzī considers this plausible for a miser.
[RAZI:104:3/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | A fourth interpretation treats the statement as an allusion to righteous deeds, which preserve their doer through good remembrance in this world and enduring bliss in the next.
[RAZI:104:3/r6] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | One reading of kalla rebukes the delusion: wealth does not make one immortal, whereas knowledge and righteousness endure; ʿAlī is quoted saying wealth keepers die while scholars remain through time.
[RAZI:104:3/r7] RAZI, d. 606 · author | reports | The second reading takes kalla to mean “indeed”; the lām in layunbadhanna answers an implied oath, conveying the force of an oath in kalla.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p88#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Akhladahu and khalladahu have the same meaning.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p88#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One interpretation is that wealth prolongs a person's hopes until he imagines it has made him immortal; the past tense portrays survival as a guarantee already settled.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p88#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الحسن | reports | Hasan remarks that death is the certain reality most like a doubt to which people give no credence.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p88#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A second interpretation is that he builds sturdy structures as someone expecting a long life or hoping to be remembered after death.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p88#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A third interpretation is an extreme love of wealth: the miser imagines losing any of it would mean dying, so he hoards to preserve life.
[RAZI-FULL:v32p88#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | A fourth interpretation alludes to righteous deeds, which preserve a person's good name in this world and bring enduring bliss in the next.

[ALUSI:104:3/r2] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Akhlada and khallada mean to leave someone lasting forever or for a very long time.
[ALUSI:104:3/r3] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | The verse uses an illustrative metaphor: wealth lengthens his hopes, so he builds, plants, and digs as if his money kept him alive.
[ALUSI:104:3/r4] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | holds | Naming māl explicitly rather than using a pronoun reinforces the point, while the past tense intensifies the intended meaning.
[ALUSI:104:3/r5] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | reports | He may literally believe wealth grants immortality through arrogance and distraction from the Hereafter, or because he thinks life and health depend on visible causes and wealth.
[ALUSI:104:3/r6] ALUSI, d. 1270 · author | rejects | A remote interpretation says the verse alludes to an actually immortalizing pursuit: working for the Hereafter; al-Ālūsī regards this as very far-fetched.
[ALUSI:104:3/r7] ALUSI, d. 1270 · عصام الدين | rejects | ʿIṣām al-Dīn suggests the miser is the subject of akhlada and wealth its object, meaning he thinks he can preserve his wealth forever; al-Ālūsī dismisses the analysis.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p230#2/r1] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The sentence is either circumstantial or a fresh sentence; akhladahu and khalladahu both mean that wealth left him everlasting, either without end or for an extremely long time.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p230#2/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | The phrase is a representational metaphor: wealth lengthens his hopes, so he builds, plants, and digs as though he thought it would keep him alive.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p230#2/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Naming wealth explicitly where a pronoun could stand increases emphasis, and the past tense intensifies the intended meaning.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p230#2/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | He may literally think wealth made him immortal because delusion and preoccupation with accumulation distract him from the terrors ahead, or because he believes life and safety depend on outward causes and wealth governs them.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p230#2/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another reading says he counts wealth among the things that grant immortality, hinting that the truly worthy pursuit is the afterlife; Alusi calls this very far-fetched.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p230#2/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | rejects | Alusi says the afterlife allusion is too far-fetched, and notes that a distinguished scholar did not treat it as an independent interpretation.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p230#2/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · عصام الدين | rejects | ʿIṣām al-Dīn proposes that the subject of ‘made immortal’ is the hoarder and its object is wealth: he thinks he can preserve it forever, unaware that mishap or death will take it; Alusi rejects the proposal.
[ALUSI-FULL:v30p230#2/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | A saying warns that a miser’s wealth should expect a mishap or an heir, illustrating that he cannot keep it forever.
[ELMALILI:104:1-9#3/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The miser imagines wealth has already made him immortal, trusts it to save him from every danger, and builds all hopes on it.
[ELMALILI:104:1-9#3/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Elmalılı rejects that presumption: lasting life comes through faith in truth, knowledge, and righteous action, as the preceding surah explained. | mentions 84:25
[QUTB-ZILAL:104:3/r1] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The wealthy person imagines money can do anything, including warding off death, securing lasting life, and escaping God’s decree and judgment.
[QUTB-ZILAL:104:3/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Obsessive attachment to wealth leads him to count and savor it while scorning people’s dignity and mocking them through words and gestures.
[QUTB-ZILAL:104:3/r3] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Islam detests and forbids mockery and faultfinding; the sura’s severe warning suggests actual polytheists targeted the Messenger and believers, but Quṭb considers reports identifying particular people unreliable.
[QUTB-ZILAL:104:3/r4] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The afterlife scene proportionately reverses the crime: the rich scoffer who imagines wealth guarantees permanence is discarded and crushed in al-Ḥuṭama, the uniquely terrifying Fire attributed to God.
[QUTB-ZILAL:104:3/r5] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The Fire reaches his heart, source of mockery, arrogance, and pride, then confines him without aid or regard, tied to a pillar like an animal.
[QUTB-ZILAL:104:3/r6] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Quṭb notes emphatic sounds and rhetorical progression—threat, ambiguity, an awe-inspiring question, and explanation—to magnify the punishment and harmonize its imagery with the mocker’s acts.
[QUTB-ZILAL:104:3/r7] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The Qur’an directs the mission while recounting it, destroying enemies’ plots and strengthening believers; God’s answer both condemns ethical degradation and reassures the oppressed that He sees, hates, and punishes their abuse.
[IBNASHUR:104:3/r1] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The clause may be a circumstantial clause describing the slanderer, used to mock his greed: nobody really thinks wealth makes him immortal, so the image is a representation or an emphatic simile.
[IBNASHUR:104:3/r2] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Alternatively, the sentence is independent and declarative for denial, or an omitted interrogative is understood, producing mockery or amazement.
[IBNASHUR:104:3/r3] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The past tense presents a future as already accomplished because the man is certain of it, intensifying the mockery as though his wealth had already secured immortality.
[IBNASHUR:104:3/r4] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The hamza in أخلده is causative: his wealth supposedly made him immortal.
[IBNASHUR:104:3/r5] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Most reciters read yaḥsibu with kasra on the sīn; Ibn ʿĀmir, ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, and Abū Jaʿfar read it with fatḥa; both are dialect forms.
[IBNASHUR:104:3/r6] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The hoarders resemble people who imagine wealth shields them from death and makes them immortal; earthly survival is their highest wish because they do not believe in another eternal life.

[IBNASHUR-FULL:v30p539/r3] IBNASHUR-FULL, d. 1393 · author | holds | The hoarder behaves as if wealth could ward off death and grant the worldly immortality that is his greatest wish, since he denies another eternal life.

[TABATABAI:104:1-3/r9] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Attachment to earth and endless hope make him crave more than life's brief needs; he mistakes wealth for immortality, and the accumulation and perceived self-sufficiency produce tyranny and superiority over others. | mentions 96:6, 96:7
[TABATABAI:104:3-6/r1] TABATABAI, d. 1402 · author | holds | Feeling self-sufficient makes a person rebel; the arrogance born of wealth's perceived sufficiency leads to fault-finding and mockery, and the causal sequence links hoarding to the warning against slander. | mentions 96:6, 96:7

[ASAD-NOTES:104:1/r1] ASAD-NOTES, d. 1412 · Asad | holds | The surah condemns slander and fault-finding alongside amassing wealth and treating it as protection that will secure immortality.
[BINTSHATI:v2p172/r3] BINTSHATI, d. 1419 · author | holds | Ḥisāb means counting materially and estimation, planning, or accountability figuratively; religious reckoning is especially associated with God.
